Dear Principal,

I heard you are deciding if everybody at our school has to do community service to graduate. I think you should require it, but only a small amount, like ten hours for the whole year. Ten hours is enough to actually help somebody and it is not so much that it takes over a person's life.

My friend Maya tutors second graders at Lincoln Elementary on Tuesdays. She says the kid she works with could barely read at the start of the year and now he reads whole chapter books to her, and she gets kind of emotional when she talks about it. My friend Jonah goes with his older brother and picks up trash along the creek behind the shopping center. He told me they filled six bags one Saturday and found a lawn chair in the water. Neither one of them was required to do any of that. They just did it.

But here is the thing. Most people are not Maya or Jonah. Most people, including me honestly, do not start something unless somebody makes them start. Last year Mr. Alvarez made our whole social studies class help with the canned food drive and I complained about it the entire week before. Then I ended up at the food pantry on a Saturday morning stacking cans, and a lady who rides my bus came in with her two little kids, and she said hi to me like it was normal, and after that I could not really think about the food pantry the same way. I never would have gone if it had not been an assignment. That is the whole reason a rule helps. It gets you through the door one time, and after that you can decide for yourself.

I also know some kids are going to say they do not have time, and they are not lying. My friend Dev has soccer practice four days a week and he watches his little sister until his mom gets home at seven. That is why I think the rule has to be fair about what counts. If a student is already babysitting their brother every day, or working at their uncle's store, or helping at their church, that should count. And we should be able to spread the hours out over the whole year instead of doing them all in one weekend, so it fits around sports and jobs.

So my position is yes, require it, but keep it small and keep it flexible. Ten hours will not ruin anybody's year, and it might change somebody's mind the way it changed mine.

Sincerely,
A student in the eighth grade

Dear Principal,

I have heard that you are thinking about making community service a requirement for every student at our school. I have thought about this a lot, because my own friends are split on it, and I have ended up believing that it should be required, but only if the requirement is small and the school helps us meet it.

The strongest reason to require service is that most students will never try it on their own. My friend Maya tutors second graders in reading on Wednesday afternoons, and she is honest about how she started: her older brother needed a ride, so she went along, and then she stayed. Nobody in our grade wakes up one morning and decides to teach a seven year old the difference between "though" and "through." Somebody has to put them in the room. A requirement is just a way of putting more of us in the room, and once we are there, a lot of us find out we like it. Maya now says Wednesday is her favorite day of the week, which is not something she would have predicted in September.

Service also teaches things that classrooms cannot. In math I learn how to solve for x. Tutoring a struggling reader teaches you that being patient is harder than being smart, and that explaining something is a different skill from knowing it. Cleaning up litter along the creek behind the baseball fields taught my cousin something too, which is that the trash does not come from nowhere. She counted eleven bottles from our own concession stand. That is a lesson about responsibility that no worksheet could have given her.

I do want to be fair to the other side, because my friends who are against this are not lazy. Devon has practice four nights a week and watches his little sister until his mom gets home at seven. If the school announced fifty hours a year, it would crush him, and he would end up faking the hours or falling behind in his classes, and neither of those helps anybody. That is why the requirement has to be reasonable. Ten hours a year comes out to about fifty minutes a month. Almost anyone can find that.

The school could also make it easier by organizing some of the opportunities itself. If there were a Saturday cleanup twice a year, a tutoring program in our own building, and a food drive in December, a student could finish the whole requirement without a car or a parent who knows the right people. Right now, the students who do service are mostly the ones whose families already had connections to it. Requiring it, and organizing it, would actually make it more fair, not less.

So my position is yes, with limits. Require it, keep it small, count a wide range of activities, and run some of it through the school. Students who already serve will not be hurt. Students who never would have tried will get a push, and some of them will keep going long after the requirement is met.

Thank you for listening to my opinion.

Sincerely,
A Student in the Eighth Grade

Dear Principal Vance,

I heard that you are thinking about making community service a requirement for all the students here, and I wanted to write and tell you what I think about it. I think you should do it, but only if it is a small amount of hours, like maybe fifteen a year, and only if we get to pick what we do.

The reason I am for it is because of my brother. He started tutoring second graders in reading last year, not because he wanted to but because his soccer coach made everybody on the team do something for the community. He complained about it for two weeks straight. Now he still goes on Thursdays even though soccer season ended in November. There is a kid named Marcus who could barely get through a whole page in September and last month he read a chapter book out loud to my brother and my brother came home and told my whole family about it at dinner. He would never have found out he was good at that if somebody had not made him try it. That is the thing about community service. A lot of people think they will hate it and then they do not.

I know some kids are going to say they do not have time, and honestly they have a point. My friend Dani has band practice two nights a week and she watches her little sister until her mom gets home at six, and she is not being lazy, she really does not have extra hours lying around. If you make the requirement too big, like a hundred hours, you are basically punishing the kids who already have a lot going on at home. But fifteen hours in a whole school year is about twenty minutes a week if you think about it that way. Almost everybody can find that. And if somebody truly cannot, there should be a way to talk to their counselor about it instead of just failing.

The other thing I would ask for is choices. Picking up litter along the highway is important and somebody has to do it, but if that is the only option a lot of people are going to hate the whole idea and never volunteer again once they graduate. Some people are good with little kids. Some people are good with old people, like my cousin who goes to the nursing home and plays cards with a man named Mr. Okafor every Saturday and knows all his stories about being a mechanic. Some people would rather do the litter cleanup because they do not like talking to strangers, and that is fine too. If the school made a list of ten or twelve places and let us choose, way more people would actually care about it instead of just signing a paper to get it over with.

I also think it would help our school. Right now when people in town talk about middle schoolers, it is usually because somebody spray painted something or was loud at the gas station. If two hundred students were out there every month doing actual work, people would have to change their minds a little. That matters for us too, because those are the same people who vote on the school budget.

Somebody will probably argue that making service required ruins it, because volunteering is supposed to be something you choose. I understand that argument but I do not agree with it. We are required to read books and some people end up loving reading anyway. Being made to do something one time does not stop you from choosing it the second time. And plenty of kids would never sign up on their own, not because they are selfish but because they never thought about it or did not know how to start.

So my position is yes, require it, but keep it reasonable and give us real choices. Thank you for reading my letter and for asking students what we think instead of just deciding.

Sincerely,
A student in eighth grade

Dear Principal Reyes,

I heard that you are deciding if every student here should have to do community service. I have been thinking about it a lot, because my friends argue about it at lunch almost every day, and I think you should require it, but only a small number of hours so it doesn't take over somebody's whole life.

First, I want to say why I changed my mind about this. Last year my mom made me go with her to the food pantry on Saturdays. I did not want to go at all. I had a whole plan for that Saturday and the plan was mostly sleeping. But once I was there I ended up sorting cans with a man named Gus who is like seventy and who told me the entire history of our town while we worked. I found out our school used to be a hospital in the 1940s. I would never have signed up for that on my own, and that is the whole point. Nobody signs up for the thing they don't know they will like. Somebody has to push you a little the first time.

My friend Dario tutors third graders at Lincoln Elementary on Tuesdays. He says the kid he works with, Milo, could not read a paragraph out loud in September without stopping five times, and now he reads whole pages. Dario is not even a great student himself, he gets Cs in English, but he is patient in a way most adults aren't. If community service was not offered through school he would have never found out he was good at that. He is thinking about being a teacher now, which is a completely different Dario than the one I met in sixth grade.

I know the other side. My friend Kayla says she already has too much going on. She has swim practice at 5:30 in the morning, she watches her little brother after school because both her parents work, and she still has to do homework somewhere in there. When people say community service "only takes a couple hours," that is a couple hours she genuinely does not have. And honestly, watching her brother IS helping somebody, it just doesn't come with a form to sign. So I understand why she is against it, and I don't think she is being lazy.

That is why I think the requirement should be small, like fifteen hours over the whole school year. Fifteen hours is less than one hour a month if you spread it out. Almost anybody can find that. And I think the school should count things students are already doing that help people, like Kayla taking care of her brother, or students who translate for their parents at appointments, or the kids who show up early to set up chairs for assemblies. If we only count the official volunteer programs, then the requirement mostly rewards students whose families have time and cars, and punishes the ones who are already carrying the most.

The other thing I would ask is that the school give us a real list of places to go. Right now if you want to volunteer you basically have to figure it out yourself, and calling a stranger and asking if they need help is scary when you are thirteen. If there was a list on the school website with places that already said yes, way more people would do it, maybe even without a rule.

Some people will say that forcing someone to help isn't really helping, because helping should come from your heart. I get that, but we force people to learn algebra too and nobody says math only counts if you wanted to do it. The food still gets sorted. Milo still learns to read. And a lot of the time the feeling comes after the action, not before it. It definitely did for me.

So my position is yes, require community service, but keep it small, count the work students already do for their families, and give us a list so we know where to start. That way it is something the school gives us instead of one more thing the school takes.

Thank you for reading this and for actually asking students what we think.

Sincerely,
A student in 8th grade

Thank you for listening to what students think before you decide.

Sincerely,

Dear Principal Barnes,

I heard you are thinking about making every student do community service to graduate. I have been going back and forth about this a lot, because both of my friends are right in a way. But if I had to pick, I think you should require it, just not a huge amount of hours.

Here is why I changed my mind about it. Last spring my older sister made me come with her to the creek cleanup behind the rec center because my mom said I couldn't stay home by myself all Saturday. I was honestly mad about it the whole car ride. But then we got there and somebody handed me a bucket and I pulled about a hundred plastic bottles and a whole car tire out of the water. There was a shopping cart in there too but it took four people to get it. By the end I actually felt good, like better than I feel after playing video games all day. I never would have signed up for that on my own. That is the thing about requiring it. Some people are not going to try something unless someone makes them, and then it turns out they like it.

My friend Devon tutors second graders on Tuesdays at the elementary school. He says the kid he works with couldn't read a chapter book in September and now he can. Devon is not even a straight A student, he gets Cs in science, but that little kid thinks Devon is the smartest person alive. You can't get that feeling from a worksheet. If community service was required, more people would find out they are good at something they didn't know about.

I do want to be fair to the other side though. My friend Alina says she doesn't have time and she is not being lazy. Her mom works nights so Alina watches her little brothers from 3:30 until 8 almost every day, and she still does her homework after that. If we made her do 40 hours of service on top of that, it would be punishing her for something that isn't her fault. And honestly, taking care of her brothers IS helping her community, her community is just her family.

So my idea is this. Require it, but make it something like 15 hours a year, and let students count things that already help people, like helping at your church or watching younger siblings or working at your family's store. Also please spread it out and don't make it all due in May, because everybody will panic and do it in one weekend and not care about it at all.

One more thing. If you make us do it, the school should give us a list of places that actually want students. My cousin at another school had to find her own place and she called six numbers and nobody called her back, so she almost failed the requirement for no reason.

Thank you for reading this and for asking students what we think.

Sincerely,
Marcus Ellery
8th grade

I heard from my homeroom teacher that you are thinking about making community service required for everybody at our school. My friends argue about this at lunch almost every week, so I already had opinions ready. I think community service is a good thing and I am glad people do it, but I do not think it should be a requirement, and here is why.

The first reason is that the whole point of helping somebody is that you picked to do it. My friend Danielle tutors second graders at Lincoln Elementary on Tuesdays and Thursdays. She talks about this one kid named Owen who could not read a whole sentence in September and now he reads her a page every time. She is proud of that. If the school made her go, it would just be another thing on her list like her bio homework, and I honestly think she would stop telling us about Owen. My cousin goes to a school in Ohio where they make you get 20 hours before senior year and she told me nobody talks about what they did, they just talk about how many hours they have left. That sounds like the opposite of caring about your community.

The second reason is that students do not all have the same amount of free time and the school does not really know what is going on at everybody's house. Marcus, who sits behind me in math, watches his little brother and sister every day from 3:30 until his mom gets home around 7. That IS helping people, he just does not get a signature for it. If you required 20 hours he would either have to find somebody else to watch them or he would fall behind, and that is not fair to punish him for. Also some kids live way out past the reservoir and their parents work, so there is no ride to the food pantry downtown and the late bus stops at 5:00. A requirement is easy for a kid whose mom can drive them on Saturday and hard for a kid who has to figure out three buses.

The third reason is that when you make something required, people find the shortest way out of it. I already saw this with the honor society hours last year. A kid I know counted mowing his own grandmother's lawn, which he was going to do anyway, and another kid's older sister just signed a paper for a car wash she barely showed up to. So the school gets a stack of forms and the community gets almost nothing. Then everybody feels like community service is fake, which is worse than not having it at all.

I do want to be fair to the other side. My friend Priya says she never would have tried volunteering at the animal shelter if her aunt had not signed her up without asking, and now she goes every other Saturday. We could have one school service day in the fall where classes sign up for a park or the food bank together, and a bus takes us, so everybody at least tries it once. And you could give people credit for it on their report card or an award at the end of the year, so the kids who do a lot get noticed. That way Priya still gets her push and Marcus does not get in trouble for raising his brother and sister.
